claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 wt% Cu during synthesis of a MnNiSi-based alloy will produce coherent Cu nanoprecipitates.
The Cu nanoprecipitates will be finely dispersed at grain boundaries.
A subsequent heat treatment will promote formation of coherent Cu nanoprecipitates in the MnNiSi-based alloy.
The Cu addition and associated precipitates will refine the grains.
Cu nanoprecipitates will impede dislocation motion.
Precipitate-mediated dislocation impediment will increase the alloy's strength.
The Cu nanoprecipitates will enhance ductility.
The Cu nanoprecipitates formed at approximately 1–2 wt% Cu will be smaller than the magnetic domain-wall thickness.
Nanoprecipitates smaller than the domain-wall thickness interact only minimally with magnetic domain walls.
Minimal interaction with magnetic domain walls will preserve the large magnetocaloric effect of the MnNiSi-based alloy.
Relative to Cu-free MnNiSi material, the Cu-modified alloy will have increased tensile strength.
Relative to Cu-free MnNiSi material, the Cu-modified alloy will have increased ductility.
The Cu-modified alloy will show no significant decrease in magnetocaloric performance.
The proposed strength–ductility–magnetocaloric balance applies only at low Cu concentrations of approximately 1–2 wt%.
Higher Cu contents may produce larger precipitates.
Larger precipitates may pin magnetic domain walls.
Domain-wall pinning by larger precipitates would reduce magnetocaloric performance.
The proposed behavior should hold from room temperature through moderate operating temperatures relevant to magnetic refrigeration.
A magnetocaloric reduction greater than 5% is defined as an unacceptable result for the proposed intervention.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes grain refinement as a strengthening mechanism, while the conditions call for comparable grain sizes between the Cu-modified and baseline samples. If grain size is held comparable, grain refinement cannot explain the predicted improvement.
